981.event_title: Aristides de Sousa Mendes issues visas to refugees in Bordeaux
981.event: In June 1940, as German forces advanced through France, Portugal's consul general in Bordeaux, Aristides de Sousa Mendes, defied his government's instructions restricting visas and began issuing transit visas to refugees, many of them Jews, giving them free to those who could not pay. Helped by two of his sons, he worked for days with little rest, and Yad Vashem records 1,575 visas issued between 15 and 22 June alone. Recalled to Lisbon, he was dismissed from the diplomatic service and died in poverty in 1954; Yad Vashem recognised him as Righteous Among the Nations in 1966.
981.explanation: Sousa Mendes treated helping desperate strangers as something his conscience simply required of him, even though it cost him his career and his family's security.
981.tie_back: The kural says that for those of perfected character every good deed is simply a duty owed, and Sousa Mendes acted on that duty as a matter of course rather than as a calculated sacrifice.
981._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of good done as duty, though the sources show he reached his decision after hesitation and soul-searching, not with the effortless ease the kural describes.

982.event_title: Eric Liddell declines to run the 100 metres on a Sunday
982.event: Learning months in advance that the heats of the 100 metres at the 1924 Paris Olympics would be run on a Sunday, the Scottish sprinter Eric Liddell, a devout Christian, declined to enter his best event and also withdrew from the relays held on Sundays. He was criticised in the press, but trained instead for the 200 and 400 metres, winning bronze in the 200 metres. On 11 July 1924 he won the 400 metres in an Olympic-record time of 47.6 seconds.
982.explanation: Liddell set his convictions above the most likely route to a gold medal, and his reputation rests as much on that choice as on his victory.
982.tie_back: The kural says the true excellence of the noble lies in character, with other kinds of excellence not counted at all, and Liddell ranked his principles above athletic glory.
982._accuracy_note: A good fit for preferring character to other excellences; the happy ending, in which he won gold anyway, slightly softens the contrast the kural draws.

983.event_title: Ashoka's Second Pillar Edict defines Dhamma
983.event: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka had a series of edicts inscribed on stone pillars across his empire late in his reign. In the Second Pillar Edict he asks what Dhamma consists of and answers with a short list: little evil, much good, kindness, generosity, truthfulness and purity, in S. Dhammika's rendering (older translations by V. A. Smith and D. R. Bhandarkar give compassion or mercy, liberality or gift, truthfulness and purity). The edict says it was written so that people might follow it and that it might long endure.
983.explanation: Ashoka set out the foundations of right conduct as a short list of inner qualities and literally carved them onto pillars for public instruction.
983.tie_back: The kural names five pillars on which perfect character rests, among them generosity, kindly regard and truthfulness, and Ashoka's pillar edict rests Dhamma on an overlapping set of virtues.
983._accuracy_note: An unusually close parallel in both image and content, though Ashoka's list includes purity and lacks the kural's sense of shame, and translations of the edict vary.

984.event_title: Eisenhower drafts a note taking all blame if D-Day fails
984.event: On 5 June 1944, hours after giving the final order to launch the Allied invasion of Normandy, General Dwight D. Eisenhower wrote a short statement to be released if the landings failed. In it he praised the troops, the air forces and the navy for doing all that bravery and devotion to duty could do, and declared that any blame or fault for the attempt was his alone. He misdated the note July 5; the invasion succeeded and the statement was never used, and it is now held at the Eisenhower Library.
984.explanation: Even in imagined defeat Eisenhower refused to place the fault on the men under his command.
984.tie_back: The kural says perfection rests on not speaking of other people's faults, and Eisenhower prepared to shoulder all blame himself rather than point to anyone else's failings.
984._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the second half of the kural; the first half, on austerity resting on not killing, is not illustrated by a wartime commander.

985.event_title: Willy Brandt kneels at the Warsaw Ghetto memorial
985.event: On 7 December 1970, during a visit to Poland to sign the Treaty of Warsaw, West German Chancellor Willy Brandt asked to lay a wreath at the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes. After laying it he knelt silently before the memorial, a gesture he later said had not been planned. The gesture was controversial in West Germany at the time, but the Norwegian Nobel Committee cited it when awarding him the 1971 Nobel Peace Prize, and it became a lasting symbol of German-Polish reconciliation.
985.explanation: A head of government humbling himself before the victims of his nation's crimes did more to open the way to reconciliation with a former enemy than any show of strength could have done.
985.tie_back: The kural calls humility the true strength of the capable and the weapon that turns enemies from enmity, and Brandt's kneeling helped change relations between peoples long divided by war.
985._accuracy_note: A close illustration of humility as a reconciling force, though the improvement in German-Polish relations had many causes beyond one gesture.

986.event_title: Eugenio Monti lends his bolt to his British rivals
986.event: During the two-man bobsleigh at the 1964 Winter Olympics in Innsbruck, the British pair Tony Nash and Robin Dixon found that a bolt on their sled had broken, and Italy's Eugenio Monti, already a multiple world champion, lent them one from his own sled. Nash and Dixon won the gold medal and Monti finished third; days later he and his mechanics also helped repair the Canadian four-man sled, and Canada won that event while Monti again took bronze. The IOC gave Monti its first Pierre de Coubertin award for fair play.
986.explanation: Monti, the established master of his sport, accepted being beaten by less decorated rivals rather than profit from their bad luck.
986.tie_back: The kural makes the willingness to accept defeat, even at the hands of those who are not one's equals, the touchstone of perfect character, and Monti chose a fair defeat over an unearned victory.
986._accuracy_note: A good fit for the willing acceptance of defeat; the rivals were not clearly his inferiors, so the sharpest edge of the kural is only partly matched.

987.event_title: Nelson Mandela invites his Rivonia Trial prosecutor to lunch
987.event: Percy Yutar was the chief prosecutor at the 1963-64 Rivonia Trial, at which Nelson Mandela and his co-accused were sentenced to life imprisonment; South African History Online notes that he had wanted the death sentence for Mandela. In November 1995, as President of South Africa, Mandela invited Yutar to lunch at his presidential residence in Pretoria and told him he had only been doing his duty as a prosecutor. Some of Mandela's former co-accused, including Walter Sisulu and Ahmed Kathrada, declined to attend.
987.explanation: Mandela used the power of his office not to settle scores but to extend hospitality to the man who had sought his destruction.
987.tie_back: The kural asks what use perfect character is if it does not do kind things even to those who have done harm, and Mandela offered kindness to the prosecutor who had helped send him to prison for decades.
987._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a personal act of kindness toward someone who had done the giver grave harm.

988.event_title: Spinoza declines the Heidelberg chair and lives by grinding lenses
988.place: The Hague, Dutch Republic (now the Netherlands)
988.event: The philosopher Baruch (Benedict de) Spinoza supported himself modestly by grinding optical lenses for spectacles and microscopes. In 1673 he was offered the chair of philosophy at the University of Heidelberg, a prestigious post, and declined it because he feared he would not have full freedom to teach and think as he wished. He continued to live simply in The Hague until his death in 1677.
988.explanation: Spinoza chose a plain, modest life of independent work over position and comfort, and his modest means did nothing to lessen his standing.
988.tie_back: The kural says that poverty is no disgrace to someone with the firmness called perfect character, and Spinoza's modest circumstances never diminished the respect in which he was held.
988._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration; Spinoza lived simply rather than in outright poverty, and the episode is also used elsewhere in the book.

989.event_title: Jan Hus refuses to recant at the Council of Constance
989.event: The Bohemian reformer Jan Hus travelled to the Council of Constance in 1414 under a safe-conduct, but was arrested soon after arriving and held in confinement. Tried as a heretic, he was repeatedly urged to recant his teachings to save his life and refused to disavow what he believed. He was condemned and put to death on 6 July 1415.
989.explanation: Hus held to his convictions even when the whole weight of the church and empire pressed on him to change.
989.tie_back: The kural says those who are an ocean of perfect character will not shift even if the ages themselves shift, and Hus would not move from his convictions even at the cost of his life.
989._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of unshakeable steadfastness; the kural's cosmic image of changing ages is matched only by the pressure of a great institutional crisis.

990.event_title: Stanislav Petrov judges a missile alert to be a false alarm
990.place: Early-warning command centre near Moscow, Soviet Union
990.event: In the early hours of 26 September 1983, Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov was on duty at a Soviet early-warning centre when the satellite system signalled that the United States had launched intercontinental ballistic missiles. Doubting the alert, partly because only a few missiles were shown, he judged it a false alarm rather than reporting an attack, and no missiles arrived. Later investigation found that sunlight reflecting off clouds had fooled the satellites; the incident stayed secret for years.
990.explanation: The steadiness of one officer at a single moment may have prevented a catastrophe for the whole world.
990.tie_back: The kural says the great earth could not bear its burden if the noble fell short, and Petrov's sound judgement helped keep the world from a disaster it could not have borne.
990._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: the event shows how much rests on individual integrity, though the kural speaks of the noble in general and of perfected character rather than of a single sound decision; the event also appears elsewhere in the book.
